design_detail: Inpatient pharmacokinetic study in 8 men, balanced crossover of two conditions about a week apart (intranasal methamphetamine 50 mg; smoked methamphetamine, 40 mg placed in the device). In each session a 10 mg dose of deuterium-labelled methamphetamine was infused intravenously over 15 minutes at the same time as the unlabelled dose, so that absolute bioavailability of the unlabelled route could be computed from the labelled intravenous clearance. Plasma was sampled to 72 hours and urine collected to 72 hours; concentrations of methamphetamine and amphetamine, labelled and unlabelled, were measured by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and analysed by non-compartmental methods. No placebo condition.
can_establish: Absolute bioavailability, peak concentration, time to peak, terminal half-life, clearance, volume of distribution and renal handling of methamphetamine and its metabolite amphetamine after intranasal and smoked dosing in 8 men, each serving as his own intravenous reference within the same session.
cannot_establish: The subjective or cardiovascular profile of either route on its own (every session also contained an intravenous dose, and the delivered doses differed between routes, as the authors state); anything about repeated dosing, women, or people who use methamphetamine more heavily; and any clinical outcome, since none was measured.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper advertisement or referral from previous participants, at a university general clinical research centre in San Francisco (pp. 476–477).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men and women aged 21 to 45 within 30% of ideal body weight, not dependent on methamphetamine by DSM-IV criteria, with methamphetamine experience at least once in the previous 6 months and experience of the intranasal, smoked or intravenous route; nobody used methamphetamine only by mouth. Medical history, examination, blood count, chemistry, hepatitis C serology and electrocardiogram excluded significant physical and psychiatric illness (pp. 476–477).
sample.demographics: 8 men completed; mean age 40 years (range 31–45). Self-reported ethnicity: 1 Black, 1 Hispanic, 4 non-Hispanic white, 2 mixed. Reported methamphetamine use ranged from 3 times a week to 3 times a year; 7 of the 8 had used all three routes and one had no intravenous experience. All smoked tobacco and used caffeine, and other illicit drug use was infrequent (pp. 477, 478–479).
sample.attrition: Eight completed; no dropouts are reported. The authors note that women were eligible but few enquired and none entered (p. 476).
sample.selection_effects: Men only, recruited by advertisement, not dependent and using relatively infrequently: a healthier and lighter-using sample than people who seek treatment, which matters for clearance, tolerance and the subjective ratings. The mean age of 40 is high for a methamphetamine laboratory sample.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered and measured in the laboratory: plasma and urine methamphetamine and amphetamine, deuterated and non-deuterated, by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, with limits of quantification of 10 ng/mL (methamphetamine) and 1 ng/mL (amphetamine) in plasma and documented within-day and between-day precision (pp. 477–478). Participants' own use was self-reported. Urine toxicology and a report of recent use were taken on admission (p. 476).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: intranasal dextromethamphetamine 50 mg (base equivalent) as a solution of the hydrochloride salt; smoked dextromethamphetamine 40 mg (base equivalent) placed in the device, of which a mean of 22.2 mg (SD 8.4, range 11.3–36.4) was estimated to have left it; and, in both sessions, 10 mg of deuterium-labelled methamphetamine infused intravenously over 15 minutes. Participants abstained from drugs and alcohol other than nicotine and caffeine for 48 hours before admission and were inpatients for 48 hours after dosing (pp. 476–477, 479).
exposure.polysubstance: All participants smoked tobacco and used caffeine, both continued; other illicit drug use was described as infrequent and was not quantified; an admission urine screen and a report of recent use were required before dosing (pp. 476, 477).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 48 hours' abstinence from drugs and alcohol (except nicotine and caffeine) before admission, with an admission urine screen; sessions about a week apart, which the authors judged sufficient because more than 90% of the drug is eliminated within 48 hours (pp. 476, 477).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own simultaneous intravenous deuterated dose is the reference for bioavailability, and the two routes are compared within person. There is no placebo condition and no non-using comparison group.
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the order of the two route conditions was balanced across participants (p. 476).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions. For the physiological and subjective measures there is no drug-free session, so pre-dose values within the session are the only baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); tobacco and caffeine use continued in all participants.

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (WinNonlin 3.0): Cmax, tmax, AUC to the last measurable concentration and to infinity, terminal rate constant and half-life, clearance, terminal and steady-state volume of distribution, mean residence time, renal clearance from 0–24-hour urine, and absolute bioavailability computed as intravenous clearance × extravascular AUC / extravascular dose. Cardiovascular monitor for heart rate and blood pressure, rate-pressure product, respiratory rate by counting; verbal 0–100 ratings of intoxication and craving and 100-mm visual analogue scales for good drug effect, bad drug effect, desire for methamphetamine and drug quality (pp. 477–478).
outcomes.validity_norms: The assay is validated in-house with stated precision and accuracy; the subjective scales are standard laboratory visual analogue scales with no norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Bioavailability' is the fraction of the administered (or, for the smoked condition, the estimated delivered) dose reaching plasma, computed against the simultaneous intravenous dose. Nothing is operationalized as harm or impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three pharmacokinetic comparisons are tested (bioavailability between routes on the nominal doses and on the estimated delivered doses; tmax between routes, after excluding one outlier) and about fourteen physiological and subjective measures were analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only; significance was set at P = .05 (p. 478).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the study was open, participants and staff knew which route was being given, and the subjective ratings are self-reports in that open condition.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD) are reported without confidence intervals. Absolute bioavailability: intranasal 79.4% (SD 13.1); smoked 37.4% (SD 14.2) of the 40 mg placed in the device, and about 67% of the estimated delivered dose (p. 481; p. 479). Peak plasma methamphetamine: intranasal 113 ng/mL (SD 23.1) at 2.66 h (SD 1.16); smoked 50.9 (SD 24.7) at 2.47 h (SD 3.91); AUC to infinity 2000 (SD 599) and 801 (SD 526) ng·h/mL (Table II, p. 480). Terminal half-life: intranasal 10.7 h (SD 2.39), smoked 10.7 h (SD 2.11), intravenous 11.8 h (SD 3.59) in the intranasal session and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) in the smoked session (Tables I–II, p. 481). Intravenous clearance 272 (SD 73.3) and 271 (SD 70.8) mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹; steady-state volume of distribution 4.30 (SD 0.930) and 4.02 (SD 0.607) L/kg; mean residence time 16.6 (SD 4.34) and 15.5 (SD 3.55) h (Table I, p. 481). Amphetamine half-life 15.2–16.9 h; amphetamine AUC 15.5–19.3% of methamphetamine AUC (Tables III–IV, p. 481). Only two P values are printed for the pharmacokinetic comparisons (P<.02 and P<.1 for bioavailability on the two dose definitions; P<.03 for tmax with one outlier excluded) (pp. 479–480).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person comparisons of means. Urine pH, which the authors note strongly affects renal clearance, was not controlled and was measured only infrequently (pp. 483–485).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The physiological and subjective data are reported mainly as a null comparison between routes, with figures rather than tables for the time courses; individual bioavailability values are not shown, only the range of the amount recovered from the device. The 67% figure (smoked bioavailability on the delivered dose) appears in the text and abstract but in no table.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 8 participants the standard deviations are large relative to the means for the smoked condition (for example AUC 801 ± 526 ng·h/mL), so the route comparison is imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Methamphetamine is well absorbed by both non-injection routes studied: about four-fifths of an intranasal dose and between a third (of the amount placed in the device) and two-thirds (of the amount estimated to have left it) of a smoked dose reached the circulation; peak plasma concentrations came at about 2.5–2.7 hours by both routes, and the terminal half-life was about 11 hours by all three routes, with amphetamine appearing later and with a longer half-life.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion conclude that exposure after intranasal or smoked use, and the possibility of drug-related complications, remain substantial, and that the findings may help risk assessment and treatment planning. This is supported for systemic exposure but not for complications, which were not measured. The abstract also reports single values (intravenous half-life 11.4 hours, clearance 272 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹, volume of distribution 4.2 L/kg, mean residence time 16 hours, amphetamine half-life 16.2 hours) that are averages or one of the two tabulated condition values, so a reader cannot match them to the tables. The time-to-peak values in the abstract (2.7 and 2.5 hours) conceal a standard deviation of 3.91 hours in the smoked condition and the exclusion of one outlier from the only test of that difference. The authors are explicit that the physiological and subjective comparisons between routes are confounded by the simultaneous intravenous dose and by unequal delivered doses, and say the intravenous tracer dose should have been smaller (pp. 480, 482, 485).

timeline.event: Smoked and intravenous pharmacokinetics in 6 men: bioavailability 90.3% of the amount that left the device, geometric mean half-life 11.1 h (smoked) and 12.2 h (intravenous)
Oral sustained-release dosing in 8 volunteers: plasma half-life 9.3–11.1 h, time to peak 5.4–7.5 h, amphetamine AUC about 21% of methamphetamine

Intravenous enantiomer study in 12 men from the same San Francisco laboratory: d-methamphetamine half-life 10.2–10.7 h, l-methamphetamine 13.3–15.0 h (shared investigators, not an independent replication)
Intranasal laboratory study with plasma sampling (Hart et al., 2008): plasma concentrations still rising at the 4-hour sample, consistent with the late peak found here

replication.where_it_stands: This is the first report of intranasal bioavailability and remains the main source for it. The half-life of about 10–12 hours is consistent across this study, Cook et al. (1993) and the oral study of Schepers et al. (2003). Smoked bioavailability differs between this study (37% of the amount placed in the device, 67% of the amount estimated delivered) and Cook et al. (90% of the amount that left the device), a difference the authors attribute to device temperature and technique; the two figures are not measuring the same denominator.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA12393 and DA00053 and contract N01DA-4-8306 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; carried out in part in the General Clinical Research Center at the University of California, San Francisco, with support from NIH grant 5 M01 RR-00079 (p. 475).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that they have no financial or personal relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research (p. 485).
funding.affiliations_note: University laboratory (Drug Dependence Research Center, Langley Porter Psychiatric Institute, UCSF); no industry sponsor.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover with each route given alone (no concurrent intravenous tracer), equal delivered doses verified by recovery, both sexes, dense early sampling to capture the rise, and urine pH measured throughout; and, for the smoked route, a standardized delivery device so that bioavailability is reported against a defined delivered dose.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two route conditions)
domains.note: The order is described only as a balanced crossover; no randomization method, sequence generation or allocation concealment is described, and no period effect is modelled.

Open administration with no placebo; each session also contained an intravenous dose that made up roughly a fifth to two-fifths of the total, and the delivered doses differed between routes, so the two conditions are not comparable for any pharmacodynamic outcome. The authors state this (pp. 480, 485).

All 8 completed both sessions, but plasma values below the limit of quantification were treated as missing and dropped from the analysis, and one participant's tmax was excluded as an outlier from the only test of the route difference.
Assays and cardiovascular monitoring are objective and validated (low on their own); the self-rated subjective measures were collected in an unblinded, placebo-free design (some concerns).

No protocol or pre-specified outcome; the headline smoked bioavailability of 67% rests on an estimated delivered dose that varied between 11.3 and 36.4 mg across participants and appears in no table; summary values in the abstract do not match either tabulated condition.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the pharmacokinetic parameters the design is strong: each participant is his own intravenous reference within the same session, which removes day-to-day variability, and the assay is validated. The overall judgment is set by the unblinded, placebo-free administration with a concurrent intravenous dose, which the authors themselves identify as making the between-route comparison of physiological and subjective effects uninterpretable. The source can be cited for bioavailability, half-life, clearance, volume of distribution, time to peak and the amphetamine-to-methamphetamine ratio by route in 8 men who used methamphetamine infrequently; it cannot be cited for the relative subjective or cardiovascular effects of the two routes, nor for any statement about complications.

key_findings.finding: Absolute bioavailability of intranasal methamphetamine (50 mg condition) was 79.4% (SD 13.1), computed against each participant's simultaneous intravenous dose.
key_findings.locator: Table II, continuation columns (F), row 'Intranasal 50 mg'

key_findings.finding: Absolute bioavailability of the smoked condition was 37.4% (SD 14.2) of the 40 mg placed in the device, and about 67% of the mean 22.2 mg (SD 8.4) estimated to have left it; the route difference was significant on the nominal doses (P<.02) but not on the estimated delivered doses (P<.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 479); Table II, continuation columns (F) (p. 481)
key_findings.note: The amount estimated to have left the device ranged from 11.3 to 36.4 mg (28%–91%) across the 8 participants, so the 67% figure rests on a mean that is itself highly variable.

key_findings.finding: Terminal half-life was essentially the same by all three routes: 10.7 h (SD 2.39) intranasal, 10.7 h (SD 2.11) smoked, and 11.8 h (SD 3.59) and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) for the two intravenous reference doses.
key_findings.locator: Tables I and II, continuation columns (t1/2)

key_findings.finding: Peak plasma methamphetamine was 113 ng/mL (SD 23.1) at 2.66 h (SD 1.16) after the intranasal condition and 50.9 ng/mL (SD 24.7) at 2.47 h (SD 3.91) after the smoked condition; AUC to infinity was 2000 (SD 599) and 801 (SD 526) ng·h/mL.

From the intravenous reference doses, clearance was 272 (SD 73.3) and 271 (SD 70.8) mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹, steady-state volume of distribution 4.30 (SD 0.930) and 4.02 (SD 0.607) L/kg, and mean residence time 16.6 (SD 4.34) and 15.5 (SD 3.55) h.
key_findings.locator: Table I, continuation columns (CL, Vss, MRT)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine appeared late and persisted longer than the parent drug: peak 9.12 ng/mL (SD 2.39) at 17.3 h (SD 5.95) after the intranasal condition and 3.71 (SD 2.88) at 15.3 h (SD 5.12) after the smoked condition, with a half-life of 15.2–16.9 h and an AUC 15.5–19.3% of that of methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Tables III and IV, main and continuation columns

key_findings.finding: Renal clearance of methamphetamine (94.4–102 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹) was about a tenth of that of amphetamine (957–1270), with a ratio of about 10 to 13; 34–39% of the dose appeared in urine as unchanged drug over 24 hours, and the Results note that the fraction excreted varied from about 10% to 90% between people.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic measures, 1st paragraph (p. 479); Tables V and VI (p. 482)
key_findings.note: Urine pH was not controlled and was measured only infrequently, and the authors attribute much of this variability to it (pp. 483–485).

key_findings.finding: Under stated assumptions (complete hepatic metabolism, hepatic blood flow 25 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹, linear kinetics), the hepatic extraction ratio was estimated at about 19%, consistent with a low-extraction drug.

In the intranasal condition, systolic pressure rose from 121 (SD 10) to a peak of 141 (SD 13) mm Hg, diastolic from 76 (SD 7) to 86 (SD 7) mm Hg and heart rate from 73 (SD 9) to 94 (SD 13) beats/min; in the smoked condition, systolic from 121 (SD 10) to 137 (SD 11), diastolic from 73 (SD 10) to 83 (SD 8) and heart rate from 76 (SD 10) to 106 (SD 19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures, last paragraph (p. 480) continuing on p. 481
key_findings.note: Both conditions also contained the 10 mg intravenous dose, so these changes cannot be attributed to the named route alone.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences in physiological or subjective effects were found between the two conditions; the authors attribute this to the shared intravenous dose and the unequal delivered doses, estimating the absorbed intranasal dose at about 40 mg and the absorbed smoked dose at about 15 mg.

In a preliminary comparison in 4 men (mean age 34, SD 9), plasma curves after 5 mg of deuterium-labelled and 5 mg of unlabelled methamphetamine given intravenously did not differ, which is the assumption the bioavailability calculation rests on.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of deuterated versus nondeuterated methamphetamine plasma levels (p. 478); Figure 1 (p. 479)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a single intravenous elimination half-life of 11.4 hours, which appears nowhere in the tables; Table I gives 11.8 (SD 3.59) and 11.0 (SD 2.68) hours for the two intravenous reference doses, whose average is 11.4.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader quoting the abstract cites a number with no printed variability and no corresponding row; the same applies to the abstract's clearance (272, the intranasal-session value), steady-state volume of distribution (4.2 L/kg, the average of 4.30 and 4.02) and mean residence time (16 hours).

reporting_issues.issue: Table I reports a time to peak of 3.55 h (SD 8.27) for a 15-minute intravenous infusion in the intranasal session, against 1.00 h (SD 0.641) for the same infusion in the smoked session. A standard deviation more than twice the mean, for a route whose peak must occur at the end of the infusion, indicates one or more aberrant values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intravenous tmax as printed cannot be used; it also casts doubt on the tmax comparison between the extravascular routes, which is reported as significant only after one outlier was excluded (P<.03).

reporting_issues.issue: All tables give the terminal rate constant λz in units of L/h; a first-order rate constant has units of h⁻¹ (the printed values, about 0.06, are consistent with h⁻¹).
reporting_issues.consequence: A units error in the table headers only; the values themselves are internally consistent with the printed half-lives (0.693/0.0672 = 10.3 h, editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a single amphetamine half-life of 16.2 hours for all routes, while Tables III and IV give 16.2, 16.9, 15.2 and 16.3 hours for the four conditions; and the abstract's renal clearances of 'about 100 and 1100 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹' are rounded from 94.4–102 and 957–1270.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the abstract's single values should not be quoted as measured parameters.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I prints the steady-state volume of distribution for the first row as '4.30 ± 0.930)', with an unmatched closing parenthesis.

Smoked bioavailability is reported against two different denominators (the 40 mg placed in the device, giving 37.4%, and the mean 22.2 mg estimated to have left it, giving about 67%), and the comparison with the 90% reported by Cook et al. (1993) is made against the second denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quoting a single 'smoked bioavailability' for methamphetamine without the denominator is meaningless; the encyclopedia must carry the denominator with the number.
